source.title: UniScale: Synergistic Entire Space Data and Model Scaling for Search Ranking
source.authors: Liron Yu; Caiyuan Li; Feiyi Dong; Tao Zhang; Zhi-Xuan Zhang; Dan Ou; Hai-Hong Tang; Bo Zheng

record.file_problem: Full paper text is present. Some tables and equations are flattened, and the conference metadata contains placeholders; neither prevents reading the study's results.
record.tranche_reason: The study applies scaling experiments to industrial search ranking and reports AUC trends, but does not test the specified language-model loss or compute-optimal-allocation claims.
record.gate_note: The study reports ranking AUC, GAUC, and HR@5, not held-out language-model cross-entropy loss. Its scale experiments and data-scaling ablations are recorded as findings about scaling in industrial ranking, not as tests of the claim versions. It explicitly says its 7× controlled sweep is insufficient to fit a power-law form.
record.test_reason: An industrial search-ranking method paper (UniScale). Its scaling sweeps are of its own architecture and measure ranking AUC, not language-model held-out loss. It fits no power law and says a 7× sweep is insufficient to fit one. It draws on LM scaling laws as motivation but bears on none of V1–V7. The reader's 'tests'/T3 contradicts its own finding that no version is tested.
record.authors_conclusion: Correct: the authors conclude that data and architecture should be co-scaled in industrial ranking and that parameter-only scaling shows diminishing returns. They present a controlled trend, not a power law.
record.recipe_differences: This is an industrial search-ranking study using AUC, GAUC, and HR@5, with data and architecture co-design; it does not use language-model held-out cross-entropy loss or fit the original language-model scaling laws.
record.method_sensitivity: The reported AUC response differs by feature-attention dimension and by whether entire-space data is paired with the co-designed architecture; the entire-space data gap over search-only data grows with model scale.

fits_no_version.finding: AUC gap between search-only and entire-space training grows from +0.12% at 40M to +0.32% at 300M. The search-only curve flattens from 100M to 300M while the ES3 curve keeps a positive slope.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: In industrial ranking models, gains from parameter scaling depend on data breadth; model-only scaling flattens sooner.

fits_no_version.finding: At 300M, scaling global feature attention gives +0.30% AUC versus +0.17% for heterogeneous attention.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: In ranking transformers, which component is scaled affects the return to parameters.

fits_no_version.finding: Naive entire-space data on the HHFI backbone gives -0.43% AUC; with DREF+DAPGA it gives +0.32%.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: In ranking, data expansion helps only with a suitable architecture.

record.problems: The authors state that the 7× controlled sweep is insufficient to fit a power-law form. The text provides only selected numerical scaling results, and does not report uncertainty for the cited AUC gains.
record.rows_left_out: Other component-ablation values and overall model-comparison metrics were omitted because they do not report additional scale trends or the key data-scaling contrast relevant to the claim.

untested.parts: All; no language-model pretraining loss is measured.
All; no fits and no extrapolation.
All for LM loss; the ranking component comparison is a different setting and metric.
Power-law form in ranking is not fitted; authors say the sweep is too small to fit one.
All; no link to pretraining loss or LM scale.
All; no exponents or fitting choices compared.

record.verdict_notes: Recommender/ranking setting with AUC metrics and no uncertainty reported. The 'scaling law' framing is motivational only. The rows are best kept as fits_no_version evidence for a recommender-scaling phenomenon, not for the LM scaling-law versions.

versions.untested_parts: Held-out language-model pretraining loss as a function of parameters, tokens, or compute.
Whether power laws fitted on small language-model runs predict much larger runs.
Loss-minimising parameter and token allocation at fixed compute, and how either scales with compute.
Loss variation from depth, width, or other architecture choices at fixed parameter count.
Whether held-out pretraining loss has the same power-law form in another modality or training regime.
Predictability of downstream task performance from language-model scale or pretraining loss.
Dependence of language-model scaling exponents or compute-optimal allocation on fitting choices, or systematic departures from fitted language-model power laws.

rows.subject: HHSFT+Search
rows.operation_detail: Scaled model size under fixed search-domain data and measured AUC gain.
rows.measure: AUC gain as model size scales
rows.value: The curve remains monotonically positive; it has a positive but smaller slope from 100M to 300M, described as flattening.
rows.note: The paper characterizes this as a controlled scaling trend, not a fitted power law; intermediate numerical values are not stated in the text.
rows.check: Monotone AUC gain over 40M–300M in ranking. No loss and no power-law fit, so it cannot bear on V1 or V5. Keep as a fits_no_version row.

rows.subject: HHSFT+ES3
rows.operation_detail: Scaled model size with entire-space data and compared its AUC gain with HHSFT+Search.
rows.measure: AUC gain as model size scales
rows.value: The curve remains monotonically positive and sustains a positive slope; the AUC gap over HHSFT+Search grows from +0.12% at 40M to +0.32% at 300M.
rows.note: The paper says the experiment is insufficient to fit a power-law form.
rows.check: Data–model interaction in ranking AUC; not a pretraining-loss power law.

rows.subject: HHSFT
rows.operation_detail: Compared scaling the global feature-attention dimension with scaling the heterogeneous feature-attention dimension.
rows.note: The paper contrasts this with +0.17% from scaling the heterogeneous feature-attention dimension.
rows.check: Component-scaling comparison inside the authors' own architecture; ranking AUC, not an LM shape test (V4).

rows.subject: HHSFT
rows.operation_detail: Compared scaling the heterogeneous feature-attention dimension with scaling the global feature-attention dimension.
rows.note: The paper contrasts this with +0.30% from scaling the global feature-attention dimension.

rows.subject: HHFI backbone
rows.operation_detail: Trained with entire-space data that naively mixes cross-domain samples, without ESUIF.
rows.note: The authors describe this as degradation from naively mixing cross-domain data.
rows.check: Method ablation (naive data mixing on the HHFI backbone, Table 4), not a scale trend. It is the study's own method compared with variants, so arguably not a claim row.

rows.subject: HHSFT+ES3
rows.operation_detail: Trained with the full ES3 data and the combined ESUIF components.

conditions.value: HHFI trained solely with intra-domain data

rows.baseline: HHFI trained solely with intra-domain data
rows.note: The paper also reports +0.26% GAUC and +0.44% HR@5 for this comparison.
rows.check: The study's own full method versus its backbone (Table 4 ablation), not a scaling measurement. Arguably should not be a claim row.

source_check.scope: Only the listed rows, labels and statements were checked; presence is not whole-study approval.
